classification.difficultyReason: List factors and identify the largest factor common to two or three whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Every part assesses finding the largest common factor by listing factors. Parts g–i use the same taught method with three numbers; hcf-two-numbers is the closest supplied skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 compares complete factor lists and identifies the largest common factor. Example 1 applies this method to three numbers. Page 3 defines factor pairs and the HCF.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List factors and identify the largest factor common to two or three whole numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: List non-zero multiples and identify the least value common to two, three or four numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses the same listing-and-comparison method. Parts g and h use three numbers; part i extends it to four. lcm-two-numbers is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 compares lists of non-zero multiples and identifies the least common value. Page 3 Example 2 applies that method to three numbers, obtaining the LCM of 6, 8 and 12 by listing multiples.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List non-zero multiples and identify the least value common to two, three or four numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Connect lists of multiples with the identification of primes and composites.

questions.mappingNote: Part a lists multiples; part b uses these lists to identify the primes below 30; part c identifies composites. Prime and composite identification is the most advanced directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces non-zero multiples by counting in equal steps. Page 3 defines primes as numbers greater than 1 with exactly two factors and composites as whole numbers greater than 1 that are not prime.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Connect lists of multiples with the identification of primes and composites.

classification.difficultyReason: List the factors of each given whole number and select those that are prime.

questions.mappingNote: Each part assesses finding factors subject to the prime-number condition. Determining factors is the primary skill; identifying primes supports the selection. Prime-factorisation notation is unnecessary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines factors through exact division. Page 3 demonstrates factor pairs and defines a prime number as greater than 1 with only 1 and itself as factors. List factors and retain the prime ones.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List the factors of each given whole number and select those that are prime.

classification.difficultyReason: Find small prime-factor products and translate repeated equal prime factors into power notation.

questions.mappingNote: Prime factorisation is the most advanced directly assessed supplied skill. The supplied preceding teaching does not establish power notation required by part c; original prior teaching remains required for its taught-method check.
questions.methodNote: Page 3 defines prime numbers as numbers greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and themselves. The factor-pair discussion supports expressing a number as a product. Parts a and b use prime factor products; part c combines repeated prime factors into powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Express small whole numbers as products of primes, then express repeated prime factors using powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Find a pair of square numbers whose sum equals each given prime, then express the pair using index notation.

questions.mappingNote: Evaluating square powers is the closest supplied catalogue skill to the directly assessed search for two squares. Identifying primes is supplied context rather than the requested response.
questions.methodNote: The inspected pages teach factors, HCF, multiples, LCM, and prime and composite numbers. They do not teach square numbers, square notation, or representing a number as a sum of squares. The authored working evaluates each proposed square and checks the sum; prerequisite method acceptance remains unresolved.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find a pair of square numbers whose sum equals each given prime, then express the pair using index notation.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret an equal-length carpeting problem as the highest common factor of three corridor lengths.

questions.mappingNote: The longest length fitting each corridor an exact number of times is the HCF of 24, 48 and 60. The existing HCF skill is the closest match, extended to three numbers as explicitly taught.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 Example 1 lists the factors of three whole numbers and selects their highest common factor. Page 3 defines the HCF as the largest factor common to two or more numbers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret an equal-length carpeting problem as the highest common factor of three corridor lengths.

classification.difficultyReason: Recognise a recurring-event problem as requiring the lowest common multiple of two visit intervals.

questions.mappingNote: The next shared visit occurs after the least positive number of days divisible by both intervals, directly assessing LCM.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces non-zero multiples and identifies the LCM as the least shared multiple. Page 3 Example 2 lists non-zero multiples to find the first common value.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise a recurring-event problem as requiring the lowest common multiple of two visit intervals.

classification.difficultyReason: Interpret three repeating lap times using their LCM, then find the corresponding clock time.

questions.mappingNote: The principal assessed method is finding the LCM of three lap durations; lcm-two-numbers is the closest available catalogue skill. Calculating the finishing clock time is secondary.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces common non-zero multiples and the LCM. Page 3 Example 2 lists multiples of three numbers and selects their first common multiple. Original prerequisite teaching for converting elapsed minutes to a clock time is not supplied.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Interpret three repeating lap times using their LCM, then find the corresponding clock time.

classification.difficultyReason: Find three prime factors of a four-digit number and verify their product.

questions.mappingNote: The task directly asks for a product of three prime numbers, making prime-factorisation the closest catalogue skill. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete task.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 finds factors by exact division. Page 3 describes factor pairs and defines prime numbers as numbers greater than 1 with only two factors. Split 1001 into factors, then split the composite factor until all three factors are prime.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find three prime factors of a four-digit number and verify their product.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose candidate prime summands, subtract to find their partners, and verify primality until every required even number is covered.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed reasoning is recognising and checking prime numbers in additive decompositions; prime-composite-numbers is the closest catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 introduces whole-number factors; page 3 defines primes as numbers greater than 1 whose only factors are 1 and themselves. Find pairs by subtraction and verify their factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find and verify prime pairs for eleven consecutive even numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct additional factors by multiplying the supplied prime factors, without division.

questions.mappingNote: The task asks for factors of a whole number; prime-factorisation is supporting context because the prime factors are already supplied.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 defines factors through exact divisibility. Page 3 connects factors with multiplication and factor pairs and defines prime numbers. Multiply distinct supplied prime factors to construct further factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct additional factors by multiplying the supplied prime factors, without division.

classification.difficultyReason: Identify the power, base and index in a supplied expression.

questions.mappingNote: The three blanks directly assess the terminology of index notation.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 names the whole expression a power, the repeated factor the base, and the superscript the index or exponent. Page 6 repeats these definitions.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify the power, base and index in a supplied expression.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate six squares by multiplying each base by itself.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts evaluate numerical squares; evaluating index notation is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Expand each square as two equal factors and multiply. Pages 5–6 establish powers as repeated multiplication and identify the square notation. They do not supply the prerequisite written multiplication or distributive calculation method.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate six squares by multiplying each base by itself.

classification.difficultyReason: Distinguish base from index and reverse familiar powers to find bases for the prescribed representations of 64.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b distinguish base from index. Part c reverses repeated multiplication to write familiar numbers as powers. Part d uses the same interpretation with prescribed indices 1, 2, 3 and 6.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines the base and index through repeated multiplication. Page 6 demonstrates positive powers, including squares and cubes, and states that a power with index 1 equals its base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Identify bases and indices and express familiar whole numbers as powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive powers by repeatedly multiplying by the fixed base; longer sequences add repetition rather than new decisions.

questions.mappingNote: Both parts assess evaluation of positive integer powers. The answer evidence confirms that each sequence starts at index 1. None of the supplied reuse candidates has the same complete task, bases and upper indices.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines powers as products of repeated equal factors. Page 6 evaluates successive powers of 3 and states that a number to index 1 equals itself. Evaluate successive powers by multiplying the preceding value by the base.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate successive positive whole-number powers by repeated multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply a specified multiplication or division law, combining only powers with the same base.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a and b apply index law 1, with b requiring identification of the two powers with base 3 while retaining the power with base 4. Part c applies index law 2 and the first-power identity.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines base and index. Pages 6–7 establish index law 1 by combining repeated factors and adding indices for the same base. Page 7 establishes index law 2 by cancellation and subtraction of indices; Examples 3 and 4 demonstrate these methods.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply a specified multiplication or division law, combining only powers with the same base.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and combine multiplication, division and power-of-a-power laws with numerical bases.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a–d use multiplication; e–g use division, including an implicit index 1 in g; h combines multiplication and division; i–j raise a power to a power; k–l apply the power-of-a-power law before multiplication or division. All directly assess numerical index laws.
questions.methodNote: Index law 1 adds indices when multiplying equal bases; index law 2 subtracts indices when dividing equal bases; index law 3 multiplies indices when raising a power to a power. Examples 3–5 demonstrate these methods. A bare base has index 1.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and combine multiplication, division and power-of-a-power laws with numerical bases.

classification.difficultyReason: Track which base the zero index applies to, then combine the zero-index rule with same-base division in the fraction.

questions.mappingNote: Every part directly applies the zero-index rule. Part g additionally uses division of powers with the same base; the grouped bases in d and h are non-zero.
questions.methodNote: Page 10 defines a^0=1 for non-zero a and explicitly distinguishes 2×6^0=2 from (2×6)^0=1. Pages 7–8 teach addition, subtraction and multiplication of indices for products, quotients and powers of powers.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the zero-index rule within products, a quotient and nested powers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate bracketed groups first and otherwise process equal-precedence operations from left to right, as explicitly instructed.

questions.mappingNote: Every part tests the effect of grouping or equal-precedence order; use-grouping-symbols is the closest supplied catalogue skill.
questions.methodNote: The order-of-operations box requires brackets first and operations of equal precedence from left to right; page 12 demonstrates left-to-right subtraction and addition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Distinguish bracketed calculations from equal-precedence operations evaluated from left to right.

classification.difficultyReason: Work backwards from target values to choose bracket placements, including grouping both sides of a division and recognising a statement already true.

questions.mappingNote: The response is a complete number sentence with brackets inserted where necessary; use-grouping-symbols is the directly assessed skill.
questions.methodNote: Page 12 contrasts expressions with and without brackets. Check proposed brackets using powers first within brackets, followed by multiplication/division and addition/subtraction.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose bracket positions to obtain specified results, including expressions with several powers and operations.

classification.difficultyReason: Select bracket placements to achieve specified results, including expressions with indices and cases requiring no added brackets.

questions.mappingNote: Each part asks for grouping symbols that produce a specified value. Parts g–l additionally assess how grouping changes the scope or evaluation of indices. The practice question continues Exercise 3C from page 13; the following 3D teaching band does not own this question.
questions.methodNote: Evaluate brackets first, then indices, then multiplication and division from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. Compare bracketed and unbracketed expressions as demonstrated before Example 8; use the multistep evaluation method of Example 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select bracket placements to achieve specified results, including expressions with indices and cases requiring no added brackets.

classification.difficultyReason: Direct application of the three taught final-digit divisibility tests.

questions.mappingNote: Question 1 directly applies the summary tests, the explanations for 2, 4 and 8, and Example 10. The closest catalogue skill is divisibility-tests, including the source-taught extension to 8.
questions.methodNote: Test the final digit for divisibility by 2, the number formed by the final two digits for divisibility by 4, and the number formed by the final three digits for divisibility by 8.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Direct application of the three taught final-digit divisibility tests.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply digit-sum tests and alternating-position sums, interpreting both zero and 11 as valid differences for divisibility by 11.

questions.mappingNote: Question 2 directly applies the digit-sum explanations, the divisibility test for 11 and Example 10. The closest catalogue skill is divisibility-tests, including the source-taught extensions to 9 and 11.
questions.methodNote: Use the digit sum to test divisibility by 3 and 9. For 11, subtract the sums of digits in alternating positions and test the difference for divisibility by 11, including a difference of zero.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the demonstrated digit-sum and alternating-position digit-sum tests.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine digit sums with parity for 6 and with the last-two-digit test for 12; the combined test for 12 is supplied.

questions.mappingNote: Each part directly applies the divisibility tests and the explanation embedded in question 3.
questions.methodNote: Use digit sums, parity and the last-two-digits test; combine the tests for 3 and 4 to test 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine familiar divisibility tests for two specified divisors.

classification.difficultyReason: Select and combine ten divisibility tests, including alternating digit sums and a large integer.

questions.mappingNote: The entire task assesses divisibility; the existing skill is the closest match even though the source also tests 8, 9, 11 and 12.
questions.methodNote: Apply the summary tests and Example 10, using alternating digit sums for 11 and combined tests for 6 and 12.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select and combine ten divisibility tests, including alternating digit sums and a large integer.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose missing digits under simultaneous divisibility constraints, coordinating suffix tests with digit sums or alternating sums and checking required exclusions.

questions.mappingNote: Constructing examples reverses the taught divisibility tests without introducing a different method.
questions.methodNote: Choose digits using the last-digit, last-two-digit, last-three-digit, digit-sum and alternating digit-sum tests, then verify every requested condition.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Choose missing digits satisfying simultaneous positive and negative divisibility conditions.

classification.difficultyReason: Infer nontrivial divisibility consequences from factors and coprime divisor pairs.

questions.mappingNote: The prepared answers establish the intended nontrivial consequences; the universal divisor 1 is not requested.
questions.methodNote: Use factor relationships and the source's combination of divisibility tests.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Infer nontrivial divisibility consequences from factors and coprime divisor pairs.

classification.difficultyReason: Combine divisibility tests to test three composite divisors.

questions.mappingNote: Tests for 12, 15 and 18 are extensions explicitly supplied by the source, within the closest existing divisibility skill.
questions.methodNote: Apply digit sums, last digits and last two digits, combining the tests exactly as explained in the question.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Combine divisibility tests to test three composite divisors.

classification.difficultyReason: Construct the smallest permitted number and justify minimality using parity and digit sums.

questions.mappingNote: The teacher answer 2232 resolves the intended use of both digits, which the prompt now states explicitly.
questions.methodNote: Use the source test for 6: even and divisible by 3; compare permitted numbers in increasing order.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Construct the smallest permitted number and justify minimality using parity and digit sums.

classification.difficultyReason: Use the digit-sum bound to determine the minimum number of digits and the smallest arrangement.

questions.mappingNote: The task reverses the taught test for 9 and requires a minimality argument.
questions.methodNote: Use the digit-sum test for 9 and place-value order to find the smallest valid number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use the digit-sum bound to determine the minimum number of digits and the smallest arrangement.

classification.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate powers of prime factors to find HCFs and LCMs of two or three numbers.

questions.mappingNote: Parts a, c, g, h and i apply the HCF method from Example 13 on PDF page 19. Parts b, d, e and f apply the LCM method from Example 12 on PDF page 19 and its introduction on page 18. The summary on page 20 confirms both rules. Prime factorisation is introduced on pages 17–18.
questions.methodNote: Express each number as a product of primes in index notation. For the LCM, take the greatest power of each prime present; for the HCF, take the smallest power of each prime common to every number.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select the appropriate powers of prime factors to find HCFs and LCMs of two or three numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Translate three equal-sharing conditions into a common-multiple requirement and determine the smallest purchase.

questions.mappingNote: The directly assessed skill is interpreting an equal-sharing situation using the LCM. The closest supplied catalogue skill is lcm-two-numbers, extended here to three group sizes.
questions.methodNote: Pages 18–19 teach finding the LCM by prime factorisation and taking the greatest power of each prime; page 20 summarises this method. Apply it to the sharing group sizes 2, 3 and 5.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Translate three equal-sharing conditions into a common-multiple requirement and determine the smallest purchase.

classification.difficultyReason: Use a prime factorisation systematically to obtain all 24 factors without omissions.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses prime factorisation and its use to enumerate every whole-number factor; HCF, LCM and root methods in the surrounding teaching are not required.
questions.methodNote: Break composite factors into primes, collect repeated prime factors and write them in increasing order using index notation, as demonstrated on pages 17–18. Enumerate products using no prime more often than it occurs in the factorisation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Use a prime factorisation systematically to obtain all 24 factors without omissions.

classification.difficultyReason: List the factors of 12 and multiply them to select the correct option.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 defines factors and demonstrates complete factor lists. Page 3 explicitly describes natural factor pairing. Finding all factors is the directly assessed prerequisite before calculating their product.
questions.methodNote: List every factor using factor pairs, then multiply the listed factors.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List the factors of 12 and multiply them to select the correct option.

classification.difficultyReason: List the factors of 18 and add them to select the matching option.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 explicitly lists all six factors of 18. Page 3 explains factor pairing. Adding that complete list directly answers this question.
questions.methodNote: Identify factors as whole numbers dividing without remainder; use factor pairs to ensure the list is complete.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: List the factors of 18 and add them to select the matching option.

classification.difficultyReason: Choose one multiple of 8 and check that the remaining amount is another; a simple split using 8 works throughout.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 introduces listing non-zero multiples; page 3 reiterates counting in the number. Each part applies that definition to multiples of 8 and verifies their sum. The selected multiplication skill is the closest supplied catalogue match for recognising the required multiples.
questions.methodNote: Find non-zero multiples by counting in the given number, then select two multiples whose sum is the target.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Recognise multiples of 8 and choose two whose sum equals each given number.

classification.difficultyReason: Find lowest common multiples of sets containing two, three or four numbers, including sets requiring extended multiple lists.

questions.mappingNote: Page 2 introduces common multiples and the LCM using 18 and 24. Page 3 Example 2 explicitly extends the listing method to three numbers. Parts a–i apply the same comparison method to two, three or four numbers.
questions.methodNote: List non-zero multiples and identify the least number common to every list. Compare common-multiple lists progressively for larger sets.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find lowest common multiples of sets containing two, three or four numbers, including sets requiring extended multiple lists.

classification.difficultyReason: Find common factors of pairs and triples, including larger whole numbers.

questions.mappingNote: All nine parts directly assess the factor-listing HCF method. The closest catalogue skill is hcf-two-numbers, extended by the source's explicit three-number example for g–i.
questions.methodNote: List factors, identify those common to every number and select the largest. Page 2 demonstrates this for two numbers and Example 1 for three numbers; page 3 describes factor pairing and defines the HCF.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Find common factors of pairs and triples, including larger whole numbers.

classification.difficultyReason: Evaluate six whole-number squares by interpreting each power as repeated multiplication.

questions.mappingNote: Each of a–f directly assesses evaluating a power with exponent 2. The repeated-factor interpretation is supplied; original prerequisite teaching for carrying in the larger multiplications is absent.
questions.methodNote: Page 5 defines powers as products of repeated factors. Page 6 explicitly demonstrates squaring as multiplication of two equal factors, including 3 squared equals 3 times 3 equals 9.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Evaluate six whole-number squares by interpreting each power as repeated multiplication.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply multiplication, division and power-of-a-power laws, including combinations of these laws.

questions.mappingNote: Page 6 explains multiplication by counting repeated factors; page 7 gives index laws 1 and 2 and Examples 3–4; page 8 gives index law 3 and Example 5. Parts a, c, d and e use addition of indices; b uses subtraction; f combines subtraction and addition; g uses multiplication of indices; h and i combine the power-of-a-power law with division or multiplication. All nine tasks directly assess numerical index laws.
questions.methodNote: For the same base, add indices when multiplying and subtract indices when dividing. Multiply indices when raising a power to a power.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply multiplication, division and power-of-a-power laws, including combinations of these laws.

classification.difficultyReason: Select greatest prime powers for the LCM and smallest common prime powers for the HCF from supplied factorisations.

questions.mappingNote: Page 18 introduces prime-factorisation LCM selection. Page 19 Example 12 explicitly takes greatest powers, and the HCF explanation and Example 13 take smallest common powers. These methods directly apply to the supplied factorisations in 8a and 8b.
questions.methodNote: For the LCM, take the greatest power of each prime present in either factorisation. For the HCF, take the smallest power of each prime common to both factorisations.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Select greatest prime powers for the LCM and smallest common prime powers for the HCF from supplied factorisations.

classification.difficultyReason: Apply the LCM to recurring events, convert minutes to seconds and include the initial simultaneous flash.

questions.mappingNote: Part a directly applies the taught LCM method to recurring events. Part b uses the same 36-second recurrence, with a duration conversion and an inclusive count. The supplied editorial decision and teacher answer establish that the initial flash is counted.
questions.methodNote: Page 2 identifies common multiples by comparing lists; page 3 Example 2 finds the LCM by listing non-zero multiples. Apply that method to the two flashing intervals. Original teaching for the minutes-to-seconds conversion and counting occurrences including the initial event is absent from the supplied relevant teaching evidence.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Apply the LCM to recurring events, convert minutes to seconds and include the initial simultaneous flash.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise a consecutive range of whole numbers and recognise the primes within it.

questions.mappingNote: The question directly assesses prime factorisation. Expanded prime products preserve the answer-book presentation; prime members of the range are identified separately.
questions.methodNote: Pages 2–3 define factors and prime numbers. Page 19 demonstrates expressing whole numbers as expanded products of prime factors before collecting repeated factors into index notation.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise a consecutive range of whole numbers and recognise the primes within it.

classification.difficultyReason: Factorise perfect squares into primes and halve their even indices to obtain square roots.

questions.mappingNote: All six parts directly apply the square-root method on page 21. Each worked solution obtains a prime factorisation, groups its even powers into a square, and evaluates the positive square root. Composite factor splitting follows the demonstrated decomposition of 324. Neither supplied reuse candidate matches this complete six-part task.
questions.methodNote: Page 6 explains repeated factors and index notation. Page 19 demonstrates prime factorisation in expanded and index form. Page 20 defines square roots. Page 21 explicitly finds square roots by prime factorisation, rewriting even prime powers as a square and halving their indices; Example 15 also demonstrates successive prime division.

previousLocalDifficulty.difficultyReason: Factorise perfect squares into primes and halve their even indices to obtain square roots.

classification.difficultyReason: Find two square numbers whose sum equals each given prime.

questions.mappingNote: Each part searches square values and checks that the remaining difference is also a square: 73−64=9, 137−121=16 and 229−225=4. This uses numerical square evaluation without introducing algebraic methods.
